title: Psychological and neural responses to architectural interiors
research_question: 1) Can aesthetic responses to architectural scenes be reduced to a few key psychological dimensions? 2) Are these dimensions sensitive to salient design features and Global Image Properties (GIPs)? 3) Do these psychological dimensions correlate with neural activation patterns, and to what extent are these correlations modulated by task?

participants.description: Experiment 1: 798 US-based adults (391 women, 401 men, 6 other), ages 18-75 (M=38.06, SD=11.96), education 5-22 years (M=15.04, SD=2.11). Experiment 2: 614 American adults (305 women, 307 men, 2 other), ages 19-72 (M=35.68, SD=10.87), education 2-26 years (M=15.26, SD=2.31). Experiment 3: 18 healthy participants (12 females, 6 males, average age = 23.39 years, SD = 4.49) from Canary Islands.
participants.recruitment: Experiment 1 & 2: Amazon's Mechanical Turk. Experiment 3: Reanalysis of previously published fMRI studies.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 200 images of interior architectural spaces, counterbalanced on perceived enclosure (open, closed), ceiling height (high, low), and contour (round, square). This yielded 8 experimental conditions (n=25 per condition): closed square low, closed square high, closed round low, closed round high, open square low, open square high, open round low, and open round high.

measures.instrument: 16 aesthetic rating scales (Complexity, Organization, Naturalness, Beauty, Personalness, Interest, Modernity, Valence, Stimulation, Vitality, Comfort, Relaxation, Hominess, Uplift, Approachability, Explorability) on a 7-point sliding semantic differential scale. Reduced to 9 non-redundant variables for Experiment 2 PCA: Complexity, Organization, Naturalness, Beauty, Personalness, Interest, Valence, Hominess, Approachability.
Pyramidal Histogram of Oriented Gradients (PHOG) method
HOG Complexity method (mean strength of gradients across all orientations)

findings.mechanism: Aesthetic responses to architectural scenes can be reduced to three key psychological dimensions: Coherence, Hominess, and Fascination.
findings.quote: The first three components were retained, given that all three had eigenvalues exceeding Jolliffe's criterion of .7 and together explained 90% of the variance.

findings.mechanism: High ceilings increase perceptions of spaciousness and prime thoughts of freedom.
findings.quote: significant main effects of ceiling height [F (1,192) = 13.56, p < .001, ηp² = .08]... on PC3 (fascination)

findings.mechanism: Humans generally feel safer in more open spaces and prefer environments affording greater visual connection with external surroundings.

mechanisms: Fluency theory (ordered arrangements increase efficiency of information processing)
Attention Restoration Theory (ART) (inherently fascinating environments are restorative, capture involuntary attention)
Prospect-Refuge theory (innate preferences for environments offering opportunities to see without being seen)
Hygge (feeling of coziness, warmth, togetherness, personal and authentic spaces)
Wholeness (spatial quality making occupants feel intimately connected)
Processing of latent psychological dimensions relies on visual inspection of scenes.
Top-down influence on object processing segregates along psychological dimensions.
Neural signatures represent top-down influences on visual valuation rather than bottom-up psychophysical properties.
implementation_implications: Architects should test the psychological impact of proposed design schemes along coherence, fascination, and hominess dimensions before construction.
The identified psychological components can be used for post-occupancy evaluations of buildings.
Architects might weigh the importance of coherence, fascination, and hominess differently depending on the building type (e.g., home, hospital, library, museum).

limitations: The use of two-dimensional images limits the generalizability of findings to three-dimensional built spaces.
The study focused on visual perception of architecture, being agnostic about the contribution of nonvisual senses to architectural experiences.
Only three basic architectural design variables were considered, which capture a limited proportion of a building's visual properties.
